lessons.title: Rhythm and two-syllable words
lessons.tip: You have every letter now. Type these two-syllable words at a regular pace, like a metronome: steadiness matters more than speed.

tuto.intro: You have every letter now. Time for rhythm: chain together two-syllable words to make your typing flow.

rules.d: Type the syllables at an even pace, like a metronome. Steadiness is better than fast, jerky bursts.
Your brain does not type letter by letter but in small groups. Feel each syllable (ba-by, lem-on, riv-er) as a single movement.
Keep your shoulders and wrists loose: tension breaks your rhythm and tires your hands.

tuto.tip: Goal: find a steady, flowing rhythm on two-syllable words.

lessons.text: baby lemon river finger table funny garden window village coffee ticket pencil

lessons.title: Essential function words
lessons.tip: Small words (the, and, but, for, with...) turn up in every sentence. Typing them in one go makes you faster everywhere.

tuto.intro: Small function words (the, and, but, for, with...) turn up in every sentence. Making them automatic helps you everywhere.

rules.d: These words make up a huge share of any English text. The more automatic they are, the faster you type overall.
Aim to type each small word in a single go, without thinking letter by letter.
Read the next word while your fingers finish the one before.

tuto.tip: Goal: type function words without hesitation, as reflexes.

lessons.text: the and but for with this that they from have will would you can not are she her his him who how

lessons.title: Common everyday words
lessons.tip: A word repeated often enough ends up typing itself. Keep your rhythm all the way along the line, even on a longer word.

tuto.intro: We widen the range to common everyday words. The bigger your stock of automatic words, the smoother your typing becomes.

rules.d: A word repeated often enough ends up typing itself. That is the goal: it frees your mind to think about the meaning.
Do not slow down suddenly on a longer word. Keep an even pace across the whole line.
If a word trips you up often, slow down on it for a few repetitions, then pick the tempo up again.

tuto.tip: Goal: chain common words together with ease and regularity.

lessons.title: Everyday vocabulary
lessons.tip: Longer words: break them into small movements, keep your typing clean rather than rushed, and let your eyes catch the end of the word while you type the start.

tuto.intro: Verbs and longer words. A chance to hold your rhythm on words with several syllables.

rules.d: A long word is typed as a string of small movements: lis-ten, car-ry, vis-it. Think in chunks.
The longer the word, the more a mistake costs you. Keep your typing clean rather than rushed.

rules.t: Look ahead to the end of the word
rules.d: While you type the start, your eyes have already caught the end. Let your fingers follow.

tuto.tip: Goal: type longer words without breaking your rhythm or accuracy.

lessons.title: First natural sentences
lessons.tip: You move on to real sentences. The challenge is no longer the key, but the flow from start to finish: type in groups of words, with the comma and full stop tucked tight against the words.

tuto.intro: You move on to real sentences. The challenge is no longer the key, but how smoothly you get from one end of the sentence to the other.

rules.d: Read and type in small groups (the children / walk / to school) rather than one isolated word at a time.
The space is hit with your thumb, without breaking your rhythm. It is the most used key on the keyboard.
The comma and full stop stick to the word before, then a space follows. Capital letters come later: for now, we write in lowercase.

tuto.tip: Goal: type whole sentences in one continuous, flowing movement.

lessons.text: the children walk to school. the teacher opens the door, and we read a book. it is a good day.
